title: Soba at the End of the Year

pages.text:
*The Owl Alley Sheet, No. 10. Today's news: the old year ended with noodles.*

The wind died by the evening bell. The air turned sharp. It was clean enough to slice.

Owl Alley crowded around Okiku's stall. Nobody wanted to buy. They wanted to wait. Long bowls of buckwheat noodles sat on low tables. Steam rose in thick, white columns. It curled around the lanterns like a shy cat. These were the noodles that would carry the old year out. Long. Unbroken. A promise that the next one would be just as long.

Umekichi and Osen carried a steaming pot of warm tofu. The blocks were pale and smooth. They looked like river stones someone had polished. Hachi, the bathhouse owner, arrived with a kettle. It was so large it looked like a small boat. The water inside was hot enough to singe the hair on his thick eyebrows. He set it down with a thud. The snow shook off the wooden roof. It landed on his hat.

Shin, the young furnace boy, sat on the lowest step. He was tired. Hauling ash all day had drained him dry. His eyes were already closed. He held his bowl in his lap. His soot-stained fingers wrapped tight around the rim. He was dreaming of a soup that never came. The alley was quiet. Only the clink of chopsticks broke the silence. And the low murmur of neighbors sharing a meal.
pages.image: A cozy, snowy night scene at a wooden food stall where neighbors gather around a low table with a large steaming bowl of noodles, Shin, a soot-stained boy in a grey jacket, sleeps with his eyes closed holding a small bowl, and warm lantern light glows on the snow.

pages.text:
Haru sat between her parents, her hands wrapped around a small cup of amazake. The sweet rice drink warmed her from the inside out. She watched the faces around her. Okiku was telling a story about a cat that had stolen a fish, and Master Ito, the ward headman, was listening with his arms crossed.

Then Okiku turned to Haru. The old woman’s eyes were bright. She held up her own empty bowl, the residue of broth still shining. "This year's best thing," Okiku said, her voice rough but warm. "She checked. She saw. She told the truth when it was easier to stay quiet."

Haru felt her face burn. The heat spread from her neck to her ears, a sudden, sharp blush. She opened her mouth to say she had only done her job, but before she could, she heard her own name in the same breath as Jiro’s.

"He is a good boy," Master Kuroda said, not looking at Haru, but looking across the alley to the dark door of his own shop. "He only wants to be seen."

The heat in Haru’s face did not fade. It cooled, slowly, into a heavy, sinking feeling in her chest. She looked at her hands. They were steady, but they felt far away, as if they belonged to someone else who was not quite there.
pages.image: Haru, a girl in a rust-orange kimono with a vermilion cord in her hair, looks down at her hands with a reddened face, while an elderly woman in a pink jacket holds up an empty bowl and a man in a brown coat looks toward a dark doorway in the background.

pages.text:
Master Ito excused himself with a small bow. He walked to the edge of the gathering, where the snow lay deep and undisturbed. Father Sota followed, his heavy footfalls crunching in the white. They stood apart from the noise of the stall, shoulders almost touching.

The headman did not shout. He spoke in a low, careful voice, the kind used for bad news that must be delivered gently. He mentioned the magistrate’s men. He mentioned the sheets sold by the street corner, the ones with no name, no permission, no register. He was not angry. His face was stern, but his eyes were worried.

"Printing is a craft," Master Ito said, his breath misting in the cold air. "But news is a power. The magistrate does not like power that he cannot see. It will not be overlooked for ever, Master Sota. You must know that."

Father Sota nodded once. He did not argue or apologize. He simply listened, his hands hanging at his sides, the small nicks on his fingers looking sharp in the lantern light. He was thinking of the blocks on the shelf, the ink in the pot, and the words that had already flown out into the city.
pages.image: Master Ito, an elderly man with a small grey topknot in a plain dark navy kimono with a wide obi and a short dark jacket, speaks seriously to Father Sota, a broad man in a wrap-front dark brown work coat and white headband, apart in the snow near a glowing wooden noodle stall at night, neighbors in quilted coats blurred behind them.

pages.text:
Father Sota walked back to the stall. He said nothing to the neighbors, and he said nothing to Mother Okiyo. He only crossed the road to where Haru sat. For a moment, his arm went around her shoulder. It was a heavy, warm weight. He squeezed once. Then he moved away.

Kichi, who had been listening from behind a stack of empty crates, finally came out. He sat down in the snow, knees up to his chest. Usually, Kichi would have made a joke about the cold, or his empty stomach. Tonight, he stayed quiet. It was the longest silence he had ever kept. It hung in the air like smoke.

Grandfather Tobei, who had been watching the two of them, picked up his chopsticks. He took a single piece of tofu. He held it up. He looked at the others.

"So," he said, his voice dry and clear. "The sheet has teeth."

He took a bite. He chewed slowly. He swallowed. He did not look at Haru. He did not look away. He just kept eating, as if the world had not just shifted under his feet.
pages.image: Father Sota, a broad calm man in a wrap-front dark brown work coat and a white headband, puts his arm around the shoulders of Haru, a small eleven-year-old girl in a rust-orange kimono and indigo apron, beside a steaming noodle stall in the snow at night, while old Grandfather Tobei in a blue-grey kimono eats a piece of tofu with chopsticks nearby.

pages.text:
The temple bell began to toll. A slow, deep sound rolled over the tiled roofs and settled into the snow. One stroke. Two. Three.

Haru counted them, just as she always did. Each note felt like a piece of the old year breaking off and falling away. Her mind drifted to the knife in her father’s hand, then to the words she had written, sharp and bright and cruel. She reached into her sleeve and touched the small, folded square of paper hiding there. It was an apology, one she had written but never given.

The bell sounded again. Outside, the wind picked up, carrying the scent of woodsmoke and ink. The alley grew quiet, the laughter faded, and steam rose into the dark sky. Haru waited for the last stroke, for the old year to end, for the new one to begin. She waited, too, to find words that were kind, and true, and enough.
pages.image: A girl in a rust-orange kimono stands in the snow looking up at a distant temple roof, her hand touching a small folded paper in her sleeve, with a large bell visible in the background and steam rising from a nearby pot.
